transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (Atlas Head of ML), Sara Klein (Eng Manager), Jonas Meyer (Infra)

---
Summary: Quick Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and caching (prefix + KV cache) and how those map to unit economics for Atlas's conversational product.

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. um we're going to walk through Optimize recommendations — batching, prefix and KV cache, and a simple cost model. feel free to jump in.
[00:15] Mark Rivera: thanks Alex. high level — we run a customer support assistant, typical chat, average user turn is about 450 tokens in, 300 tokens out, and peak concurrency is around 120 rps during US hours.
[00:30] Priya Patel: okay got it, that's helpful. so two main levers: batching and caching. batching reduces GPU utilization per token via amortization, caching avoids regen for repeated prefixes or long contexts.
[00:45] Sara Klein: quick question — how much latency hit do we take when we batch? our SLA target is p95 < 400ms for single-turn flows.
[01:05] Priya: good q. it depends on batching policy. for latency-sensitive routes we recommend a short max wait window (e.g., 10-20ms) and small target batch sizes (8-16) so you get throughput wins with minimal added tail latency. in our tests with sequence lengths similar to yours we saw p50 latency maintain around 120-160ms with batch=16 and 15ms window; p95 nudges up ~40-80ms depending on model.
[01:35] Jonas Meyer: are those numbers for hosted or dedicated? we care about predictable throughput.
[01:45] Priya: these are runtime numbers on our dedicated pools with NVIDIA H100-like hardware; for hosted they look similar but with more variability because of multi-tenant scheduling. dedicated typically gives you tighter p95 and better cost per token at scale.
[02:00] Mark: can you walk through a simple cost calc? we want to compare hosted vs dedicated and the impact of batching + KV cache.
[02:15] Alex: sure; we'll use round numbers to keep it simple. assume model cost baseline (hosted) is $0.10 per 1k input tokens + $0.15 per 1k output tokens — so ~$0.25 per 1k tokens total, just example numbers.
[02:35] Alex: for Atlas average request total tokens = 450 + 300 = 750 tokens. at $0.25 per 1k, per-request cost is 0.75 * 0.25 = $0.1875. that's about $0.19 per request. at 120 rps sustained that's ~10.4M requests/day — (editor's note: quick mental math, actually 120 rps * 3600 * 24 = 10,368,000 req/day) which is huge, so batching and cache matter a lot.
[03:05] Priya: now batching: if you can batch 16 requests and the runtime achieves 3.8x token throughput efficiency vs single-request serving, your per-token cost drops roughly by 3.8x on GPU time component. so effective per-request cost would be $0.1875 / 3.8 ≈ $0.049.
[03:25] Sara: wow that's big. how realistic is the 3.8x? what assumptions?
[03:35] Priya: that comes from 1) continuous batching kernel throughput improvements on attention, 2) more efficient kernel launch amortization and 3) memory and kv-cache packing. it's realistic for medium-length sequences on modern backends; your actual will depend on distribution of sequence lengths and how bursty your traffic is.
[03:50] Mark: ok what about caching — prefix vs KV cache. can you clarify difference and what to use where?
[04:05] Priya: yes. prefix caching is essentially caching of the tokenized prefix — think system prompts, instructions, or repeated context snippets. it's good when the same prefix repeats across many requests. KV cache is the transformer key/value cache that speeds up autoregressive generation for long contexts — it's useful to avoid recomputing long histories when users have long chats. KV cache is session-local and speeds up generation, whereas prefix cache can be shared across requests.
[04:35] Jonas: example: we have a lot of similar legal disclaimers + user metadata included in each prompt — that's probably prefix cache territory?
[04:45] Priya: exactly — put the static parts into a cached prefix. for user-specific history that grows, use KV cache or partial checkpointing, so you don't re-encode entire history every time.
[04:58] Mark: any numbers for cache hit rates and cost impact?
[05:05] Alex: yes — simple example: if 40% of tokens are repeated prefixes, and you can cache those, you'll reduce token compute by 40% for those requests. combined with batching efficiency, you multiply wins. e.g., 40% token reduction + 3.8x batching = per-request cost drop from $0.1875 to ~ $0.1875 * 0.6 / 3.8 ≈ $0.0296. so around $0.03 per request in this simplified model.
[05:35] Sara: that seems almost too good to be true. what are the tradeoffs? storage? eviction? cache staleness?
[05:45] Priya: tradeoffs: prefix cache needs a small fast store (and can be memory-backed) and TTL/invalidations; KV cache consumes GPU memory per session — so session concurrency impacts GPU capacity. eviction policies, LRU, TTL, and shard sizing matter. also security: if you're in private deployment, you control KMS and keys; hosted we'll do tenant isolation plus audit logs.
[06:10] Jonas: how do you size KV cache memory? like, if we have 10k concurrent sessions with average history of 4k tokens each, how do we estimate GPU memory needs?
[06:25] Priya: rough calc: KV cache per token per head uses X bytes — (note: Priya gives approximate numbers but voice fuzzes) — with 32-head mm, 2048 dims it's about ~0.5–1KB per token depending on precision and quantization. so 4k tokens * 1KB ≈ 4MB per session. 10k sessions => 40GB, which maps across GPUs and nodes. with quantization + eviction you can reduce. that's why we often use prefix caches to avoid storing huge per-session KV state and only keep recent active sessions hot.
[07:00] Mark: got it. can Redwood do automatic cache population and routing?
[07:05] Priya: yes. Optimize can suggest keys to prefix cache (common system prompts), and runtime has policies to route cache hits to hot nodes. we also have auto-eviction heuristics based on access freq and recency.
[07:18] Sara: security: our compliance folks ask about encryption at rest for the cache and KMS integration — is KV cache encrypted and auditable?
[07:28] Alex: for Private customers we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. in hosted mode cache metadata is tenant-isolated and encrypted at rest; we can share SOC2 and encryption docs.
[07:45] Mark: please share those docs.
[07:48] Alex: will do, action item.
[07:50] ---
[08:00] Priya: back to practical tuning. I usually recommend a 3-step approach: 1) pick latency tier (fast vs standard), 2) set batching window and max batch size (fast: 10-20ms window, size 8-16; standard: 30-50ms window, size 16-32), 3) enable prefix caching for static parts and set KV cache for active session state with TTL like 6–24 hours depending on session reuse.
[08:30] Jonas: TTL 24h seems long; storage cost?
[08:35] Priya: yes longer TTL increases memory footprint; many customers choose 1–6 hours for chat apps. 24h is for apps where users return infrequently and maintaining state is critical. we can simulate expected memory growth during the pilot.
[08:50] Mark: what's the recommended pilot configuration you mentioned?
[08:55] Priya: pilot config we typically propose: 2-week run, mirror production traffic with a 10% synthetic load to protect prod, target routes: web chat and email summarization, enable batch=16 with 15ms window for chat route, prefix cache for shared system prompts, KV cache TTL=6h, measure p50/p95, token cost, and cache hit rate. Redwood will give a load script and cost spreadsheet.
[09:25] Sara: what about request signatures and cache keys — how do we compute keys safely so PII isn't leaked?
[09:35] Priya: great callout — cache keys are generated from non-PII hashed digests; we recommend canonicalization of prompts to remove sensitive user identifiers before caching. you can also encrypt keys and use tokenization steps to strip PII.
[09:55] Mark: any gotchas with function-calling or tool-calls interfering with caching?
[10:05] Priya: function-calls often depend on dynamic tool outputs, so unless tool output is stable across requests you shouldn't prefix-cache that portion. we support partial caching where stable prefix is cached and dynamic sections are appended. there can be edge cases with non-determinism and stochastic outputs — watch those routes.
[10:30] Alex: quick interrupt — we also wanted to call out model variants: for high-volume low-sensitivity calls you can drop to a quantized variant or a smaller family and push sensitive or high-quality requests to the high-accuracy model. routing policy reduces cost further.
[10:45] Jonas: do you have a sample cost comparison hosted vs dedicated with batching + caching included?
[11:00] Alex: yes I'll share a sheet, but here's a slide-of-sorts: hosted baseline per-request $0.19; hosted + 40% prefix cache hit + batch 16 -> ~$0.03. dedicated fixed commit reduces per-token cost 40–60% depending on commit, so the same optimizations on dedicated could push per-request cost to ~$0.02 or lower once committed capacity is amortized. main tradeoff: reserved spend upfront vs lower unit cost.
[11:30] Mark: interesting. for our procurement team, what SLA/uptime do you commit for Dedicated?
[11:40] Alex: Dedicated comes with an SLA — typical is 99.9% plus latency SLOs per route. we'll attach current SLA language and uptime history in the follow-up.
[11:55] Sara: can we run a benchmark with our private VPC? security would prefer private deployment for sensitive workflows.
[12:05] Alex: yes, we have Private deployment options. for the pilot we can do a Private pilot in your VPC or a dedicated hosted pilot — depends on procurement schedule. Private gives you more control over KMS and network egress.
[12:20] Mark: procurement timeline is 6–8 weeks, so a hosted pilot might be faster to start.
[12:25] Priya: that works — we can configure pilot on hosted dedicated pool but with tighter isolation and retention controls to meet security needs while procurement moves.
[12:35] Sara: ok next steps then?
[12:40] Alex: action items: we'll send the cost model sheet and pilot config, Priya will send the sample load script and suggested batch/cache params. Jonas will give us actual traffic metrics. we'll reconvene after we have pilot metrics — propose day 3 deep-dive and a wrap at the 2-week mark.
[12:55] Mark: sounds good. also please add SOC2 and KMS docs in the email.
[13:00] Alex: will do.

(there's some light cross talk as people drop into side channels, small transcription noise)

[13:30] Priya: a couple of tuning tips before we end: 1) reduce max batch wait for latency-sensitive paths, 2) use adaptive batching during low traffic, 3) proactively pre-warm hot shard nodes when you expect spikes, 4) instrument token-level cost telemetry in your app to measure wins.
[13:55] Jonas: how do we instrument token-level telemetry? do you provide SDK hooks?
[14:05] Priya: yes we provide SDK hooks and tracing that reports per-request token breakdown, model, batch size, and cost attribution. these integrate into your observability stack and Redwood Console for dashboards.
[14:20] Alex: ok, thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and docs. appreciate the time.
[14:30] Mark: thanks, appreciate it.

End of meeting.
